sources.title: Josephine Butler (Q225863), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-11-18): English label 'Josephine Butler', description 'British feminist and social reformer fighting to end child prostitution (1828-1906)', instance of human, born 13 April 1828, died 30 December 1906, citizenship United Kingdom and Great Britain, no Korean label. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

Krista Cowman, 'Butler, Josephine', Encyclopedia of Modern Europe: Europe 1789-1914 (Gale, reproduced on Encyclopedia.com; read in full with its bibliography). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: names her a British feminist activist best known for leading the Ladies National Association for the Repeal of the Contagious Diseases Acts from 1869, a campaign that ended in victory in 1886 at great personal cost (ridiculed and physically attacked on speaking tours); records her first rescue case in Oxford (a young woman held in Newgate for infanticide, offered a position), her workhouse visits and home rescue work in Liverpool from 1866 after the death of her daughter, her presidency of the North of England Council for the Higher Education of Women, her 1868 pamphlet on the education and employment of women, her extension of the campaign to child prostitution and a tour of Europe, the 1885 rise of the age of consent from thirteen to sixteen, the damage to her husband's career and the annuity raised by friends, and her paper The Storm Bell after 1890. Short scholarly reference entry by a historian of women's activism; admiring on motive.

Tony Little, 'Josephine Butler, 1828-1906', Journal of Liberal History (political-history biography; read in full). INDEPENDENT POLITICAL-HISTORY VOICE: says her willingness to speak publicly on sexual issues distracted from her wider views; records that in 1869 Elizabeth Wolstenholme Elmy invited her to be honorary secretary of the new Ladies National Association, that she hesitated and wrote to her husband for permission, that George Butler's career was damaged, that she became the campaign's figurehead and treated prostitutes as equals; the 1870 Colchester and 1872 Pontefract by-election tactics of splitting the Liberal vote, which he judges counterproductive because the campaign's parliamentary support came from Liberals and it stalled when Gladstone fell in 1874; her turn to a Europe-wide crusade, the 1883 suspension and 1886 repeal with James Stansfeld as parliamentary spokesman, her cooperation with W. T. Stead's 1885 Maiden Tribute exposure, and her later distancing from the National Vigilance Association's puritanical campaigns; also her work on women's education and married women's property.

Paula Bartley, 'Butler, Josephine (1828-1906)', Women in World History: A Biographical Encyclopedia (Gale, reproduced on Encyclopedia.com; read in full). Longer encyclopedia entry drawing on Butler's own memoirs and Judith Walkowitz's scholarship, so partly self-report: first-year travel of 3,700 miles to 99 meetings, the sale of her jewels for the cause, a petition of 250,000 women in 1871, the mud, flour and furniture thrown at repealers in Colchester, an MP's remark that they were worse than prostitutes, the 1874 tour of France, Italy and Switzerland, her persuasion of Rebecca Jarrett to take part in Stead's 1885 exposure, her part in founding the National Vigilance Association and later withdrawal as it grew repressive, her criticism of the attempt to reintroduce compulsory examination in India, and The Storm Bell (1898). Gives a different age-of-consent figure (twelve to sixteen) and an earlier date for her daughter's death than the other sources; those details are not used. Admiring.

Helen Mathers, review of Jane Jordan's biography 'Josephine Butler' (John Murray, 2001), Times Higher Education, 1 March 2002 (read in full). Describes Jordan as the first biographer to research the whole Butler archive and warns that the archive risks telling the story entirely from Butler's point of view, that Jordan is not always critical enough, and that the literal truth of some of Butler's 'highly coloured, emotive and propagandist prose' is questionable. Records the contemporary hostility (a canon of St Paul's called her 'that dreadful woman'; Benjamin Jowett thought prostitutes a class she had better have left alone), her skill as a public speaker and writer, her evangelical conviction that men and women are of equal worth, her ministry to women picking oakum in the Liverpool workhouse and her House of Rest, and her supplying evidence on child prostitution to the 1885 Maiden Tribute campaign. Scholarly review, admiring of its subject, critical of the biography's use of sources.

Lucinda Matthews-Jones, "'Granny thinking what she is going to write in her book': religion, politics and the Pontefract by-election of 1872 in Josephine Butler's Personal Reminiscences of a Great Crusade (1896)" (scholarly article, Liverpool John Moores University repository; read in full). CRITICAL VOICE: compares Butler's memoir with the repeal movement's own papers and with the press, and finds that she appears on the periphery of the by-election while the back-stage organising was done by Henry Wilson, that the by-election turned on the secret ballot and the two candidates rather than on her, that her hayloft account (cayenne pepper, burning hay, an attack on the meeting) is hard to verify and exaggerated in places though Wilson's letter and The Shield confirm a meeting broken up by 'roughs', and that she shifted her account of the Liberal candidate Hugh Childers after he later supported repeal; quotes the Saturday Review calling the women 'indecent Maenads'. Also records her aversion to publicity and to biography.

University of Liverpool Library, Special Collections and Archives, 'Josephine Butler Collection' (library guide; read in full). Institutional description of the national collection of her papers: says that, under her leadership, the Ladies' National Association led the campaign that ended in repeal in 1886, that she was a major figure in the federation founded in 1875 that became the International Federation for the Abolition of State Regulation of Vice, that she held independent views on Irish Home Rule, the Boer War, women's suffrage and slavery that she aired in books, pamphlets and letters, and that her husband supported her campaigning at the expense of his own career; also her commemoration in Liverpool (Noble Women windows, the Josephine Butler Memorial House, 1920 to 1972). Holder of the archive; commemorative in tone.

Northumberland Archives, 'Josephine Butler Timeline' (archive learning resource; read in full). Dated sequence from her 1828 birth to her death on 30 December 1906: marriage in 1852, the death of her daughter Eva and the 1866 move to Liverpool, her signature on the 1866 women's suffrage petition, the 1868 pamphlet, the founding of the Ladies National Association in 1869 after women were barred from the men's National Association, the first issue of The Shield in 1870, the 1875 International Abolitionist Federation, the 1883 suspension and 1886 repeal, the 1885 Criminal Law Amendment Act raising the age of consent from thirteen to sixteen, George Butler's death in 1890, and The Storm Bell (1898-1900) with her views on prostitution in India. Local archive timeline; used mainly for consistent dates.

The Salvation Army International Heritage Centre, 'Josephine Butler, Florence Booth and The Maiden Tribute of Modern Babylon' (heritage-centre blog, December 2017; read in full). INTERESTED INSTITUTIONAL VOICE: says that after Butler wrote in support of the Salvation Army when it met opposition in Switzerland in 1883 she formed a close association with Florence Booth; that, according to Bramwell Booth's memoirs, Butler was a consultant in the 1885 Maiden Tribute exposure and in deciding when to publish, while noting that the mastermind is unclear; that Stead and Rebecca Jarrett were convicted over the Eliza Armstrong 'purchase' and Bramwell Booth acquitted; that Butler's article in The War Cry defended the abduction as 'pretended' and carried out at great risk for moral reform; that Jarrett went to a Butler rescue home in Winchester; and that the Criminal Law Amendment Act of 1885 raised the age of consent from thirteen to sixteen.

persistence.rationale: [src_butler_cowman, src_butler_little, src_butler_bartley, src_butler_nro | 1869-1900 | reference entry, journal biography, encyclopedia entry, archive timeline] Four sources describe a campaign that ran from the founding of the Ladies National Association in 1869 to repeal in 1886 despite ridicule, physical attack and a stall after 1874, with her work on the Continent, in India in the 1890s and in her paper The Storm Bell (1898) after that. Repeal was a collective and political result (Little credits Stansfeld and the Stead exposure), so the outcome is not scored, only the sustained effort. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 80 / 0.66 to 78 / 0.64 because the encyclopedia detail (3,700 miles, sold jewels) is drawn from her own memoir tradition and the end result was a shared one.

conflict_tolerance.rationale: [src_butler_bartley, src_butler_mathers, src_butler_mjones, src_butler_little | 1869-1872 | encyclopedia entry, scholarly review, scholarly article, journal biography] She spoke publicly on a taboo subject and kept at it after personal attack: Colchester repealers were pelted with mud, flour and furniture, a canon of St Paul's called her 'that dreadful woman', Jowett disapproved, the Saturday Review called the women 'indecent Maenads', and her husband's career suffered. Wilson's contemporary letter and The Shield confirm that her Pontefract meeting was broken up by 'roughs', although the scholarly article shows her own hayloft account is exaggerated. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 80 / 0.66 documented to 76 / 0.62 strong inference because the most vivid episode is her own retelling and the surviving contemporary evidence is thinner.

proactive_agency.rationale: [src_butler_cowman, src_butler_little, src_butler_bartley, src_butler_mathers | 1850s-1869 | reference entry, journal biography, encyclopedia entry, scholarly review] Without being asked she took a woman held for infanticide into her household in Oxford, began visiting the Brownlow Hill workhouse in Liverpool, took inmates into her home and later ran a House of Rest and an industrial home, and joined the higher-education council and the married women's property committee. The LNA role itself came by invitation, which Little records she hesitated over. CONCENTRATION (agent): lowered from 78 / 0.62 to 76 / 0.6 because the House of Rest and industrial home details rest on the memoir-derived encyclopedia entry and the Jordan-based review.

leadership_drive.rationale: [src_butler_little, src_butler_cowman, src_butler_liverpool, src_butler_mjones | 1867-1886 | journal biography, reference entry, library archive guide, scholarly article] She presided over the North of England Council (1867-73) and the Ladies National Association and was a major figure in the 1875 federation. Little notes that she hesitated and sought her husband's permission when invited in 1869, and Matthews-Jones shows that at Pontefract much organising was done by Henry Wilson while her memoir places her at the centre. She is better evidenced as the movement's figurehead than as its sole organiser. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 72 / 0.58 to 68 / 0.54 because the central-leader picture partly comes from her own memoir.

persuasiveness.rationale: [src_butler_mathers, src_butler_bartley, src_butler_little, src_butler_mjones | 1869-1885 | scholarly review, encyclopedia entry, journal biography, scholarly article] Sources call her an impressive speaker and writer who drew large audiences and a petition of 250,000 women in 1871; the MP remark that her revolt was 'very awkward' is in her own recollection. Matthews-Jones notes the repealers did not defeat Childers at Pontefract and Little judges the by-election strategy counterproductive, so audience effect and political result are not the same. CONCENTRATION (agent): lowered from 72 / 0.56 to 68 / 0.5 because the praise is admiring or memoir-derived.

impact_motivation.rationale: [src_butler_cowman, src_butler_bartley, src_butler_mathers, src_butler_nro | 1860s-1900 | reference entry, encyclopedia entry, scholarly review, archive timeline] Her work was aimed at the welfare and legal standing of women: rescue work and workhouse visits, repeal of the Acts, child protection and women's education, continued until her husband's death and after, at cost to his career and her own money. Sources describe grief as an initial spur and an evangelical belief in equal worth as the ground, which are her own explanations. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 78 / 0.6 to 74 / 0.56 because the motive evidence is largely her own writing as relayed by admiring biographers.

independent_thinking.rationale: [src_butler_liverpool, src_butler_little, src_butler_bartley, src_butler_sa | 1883-1900 | library archive guide, journal biography, encyclopedia entry, heritage-centre blog] The Liverpool guide says she held independent views on Irish Home Rule, the Boer War, women's suffrage and slavery; Little and Bartley record that she disassociated herself from the National Vigilance Association's repressive turn and criticised official regulation in India; she publicly defended Stead and Jarrett when others condemned them. CONCENTRATION (agent): lowered from 70 / 0.54 to 66 / 0.5 because the Home Rule and Boer War positions are a single library summary line with no stated stance, and the NVA withdrawal appears in two entries that read alike.

collaboration.rationale: [src_butler_little, src_butler_cowman, src_butler_mjones, src_butler_sa | 1867-1892 | journal biography, reference entry, scholarly article, heritage-centre blog] She worked with Elizabeth Wolstenholme Elmy, Anne Clough and Lydia Becker on women's causes, with Stansfeld in Parliament, with James Stuart, Henry and Charlotte Wilson in the Pontefract campaign, and with Stead and Florence Booth on the 1885 exposure. Different sources name different partners and Matthews-Jones shows a team rather than a lone figure; how decisions were shared is not described, so the score is moderate.

risk_tolerance.rationale: [src_butler_little, src_butler_cowman, src_butler_sa | 1869-1885 | journal biography, reference entry, heritage-centre blog] She accepted public hostility, risk to her husband's career and association with Stead's staged 'purchase' of a girl, for which Stead and Jarrett were convicted; the heritage-centre blog says her role rests on Bramwell Booth's memoir and calls the mastermind unclear. Exposure is documented, but no source describes how she weighed it. CONCENTRATION (agent): lowered from 64 / 0.46 to 60 / 0.42 because the Maiden Tribute involvement depends on one memoir quoted by an interested institution.

adaptability.rationale: [src_butler_little, src_butler_cowman, src_butler_nro | 1874-1898 | journal biography, reference entry, archive timeline] When the by-election campaign stalled after the Liberal government fell in 1874 she turned to a Continental campaign and the 1875 federation, then to child prostitution after 1883 and to India in the 1890s. Only Little describes the 1874 turn as a response to a setback; the other sources list activities. CONCENTRATION (agent): lowered from 64 / 0.5 strong inference to 60 / 0.46 inference because the pivot rests on one source.

portrait.source: Frontispiece plate of Josephine E. Butler: An Autobiographical Memoir, edited by George W. and Lucy A. Johnson (Bristol: J. W. Arrowsmith, 1909), captioned '(after) G. Richmond, A.R.A., circa 1852' with the engraver's mark of the Swan Electric Engraving Co. Ltd, and listed in the book's illustrations as 'Josephine Butler, circa 1852. Frontispiece'; scan at the Internet Archive (josephineebutler00butliala), leaf 4 (1924 x 3402 pixels). The file is the printed picture cropped from the page, converted to greyscale and downscaled to 686 x 1000 with no upscaling. The plate reproduces George Richmond's pastel portrait, which Wikimedia Commons identifies as the National Portrait Gallery's Josephine Butler (dated 1851 there); the National Portrait Gallery record itself could not be opened (HTTP 403).
portrait.license: Public domain: the underlying pastel is by George Richmond (died 1896) and the plate was published in the United Kingdom in 1909 (before 1931); a faithful photo-mechanical reproduction of an old two-dimensional work adds no new rights; the Internet Archive item is marked not in copyright; holder (National Portrait Gallery) terms were not readable

Frontispiece') and the plate itself, which is captioned '(after) G. Richmond, A.R.A., circa 1852' with the Swan Electric Engraving Co. mark; the Internet Archive item is marked NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT. The shipped file is that printed plate cropped and downscaled (686 x 1000), not the NPG or Commons file. Rights basis: Richmond died 1896 and the plate was published in 1909. KIND likeness: a pastel drawn about a year before her 1852 marriage; the plate is a reproduction, and the NPG's own date (1851) and the plate's circa 1852 differ slightly, so the date is given as about 1851-52. Not used: the Elliott and Fry c.1880 LSE photograph (fallback, only a generic no-known-restrictions statement) and the 1869 'saintlaika.com' and 1894 Watts items (unsupported or with third-party claims). Also read and not cited: Christian History magazine piece (hagiographic, errors), LSE Library highlights page (short, used only to check dates), the 1909 memoir OCR (only its illustration list and frontispiece). PERSPECTIVES: (1) academic reference entry; (2) political-history biography; (3) encyclopedia entry leaning on her own memoirs; (4) a review that questions how biographers use her archive; (5) a source-critical scholarly article comparing her memoir with press and movement papers; (6) two archives; (7) an interested religious-institution blog. NON-SELF BEHAVIOURAL SOURCES: Cowman, Little, Matthews-Jones (press and movement papers) and the Liverpool and Northumberland archive pages; Bartley, the Mathers review (of a biography built on her papers) and the Salvation Army blog lean on her or her allies' accounts. CONTRADICTIONS AND LIMITS: age of consent before 1885 is thirteen (Cowman, Northumberland, Salvation Army) or twelve (Bartley); her daughter's death is 1864 (Northumberland, Little) or 1858 (Bartley); Cowman's entry has a slip (son born 1882 for 1852); founding of the 1875 federation is 'founded by' (Northumberland, LSE) or 'major figure' (Liverpool); her role in the Maiden Tribute exposure is uncertain (Bramwell Booth memoir: consultant; the blog calls the mastermind unclear; Bartley: she persuaded Jarrett). None of these is carded as fact. Her hayloft account at Pontefract is not carded as fact either. No adversarial full-length biography found; the critical voices are Matthews-Jones (her centrality and her memoir's reshaping), Little (the electoral tactics were counterproductive), Mathers (biographers too reliant on Butler's own account) and Bartley's note that by 1900 rescue work was heavily criticised.
